findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for External Auditor's Annual Report 2025/26
findings.headline: Monitoring Officer and Corporate Director of Children's Services left after year-end and were replaced by interims
findings.detail: The paper says the interim Director of Children's Services was appointed permanently. It also notes the new Chief Executive and Leader appointed during 2025/26.
findings.matters: A finance director or peer council can see the leadership turnover in the children's and governance roles, which the paper ties to the Council's delivery priorities.
findings.quote: Post year end, the latter two officers have left the Council and replaced by Interims

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for External Auditor's Annual Report 2025/26
findings.headline: Auditor has not yet reached conclusions on the 2025/26 financial statements or other information
findings.detail: The paper says the auditor issued the Annual Report before completing work on the financial statements and other information, to meet the 30 November deadline. The Whole of Government Accounts procedures are also not confirmed as complete.
findings.matters: A lender or finance director reading the report needs to know the accounts opinion is outstanding, and that the timing reflects the Code of Audit Practice deadline.
findings.figures: Auditor's Annual Report due by 30 November; accounts opinion pending
findings.quote: Consequently, we have not reached our conclusions in respect of these areas.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for External Auditor's Annual Report 2025/26
findings.headline: Auditor identifies no significant weaknesses in value for money arrangements for 2025/26
findings.detail: The paper says the auditor identified a significant value for money risk on EHCP arrangements, which did not materialise into a significant weakness. The conclusion is based on the stabilised EHCP performance, the in-house transition plan and the action plan for failed services.
findings.matters: A finance director can see the auditor's value for money conclusion for the year, and a lender reads it as an absence of a significant weakness on governance or performance arrangements.
findings.figures: no significant weaknesses identified; 3 criteria assessed
findings.quote: We identified no significant weaknesses in respect of the arrangements the Council has put in place

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for External Auditor's Annual Report 2025/26
findings.headline: Overdue EHCPs over 20 weeks old fell from approximately 1,600 to 740 by late Summer 2026
findings.detail: The paper says 6% of EHCPs met the 20-week statutory target in 2025/26, with performance stabilising during the year as the Council prioritised the oldest cases. Since year-end, around 150 to 300 plans a month have been processed, with outsourced educational psychologists used for assessments.
findings.matters: A finance director or peer council with a SEND backlog can compare the monthly processing rate and the outsourcing approach, and the paper links the backlog to tribunal risk.
findings.figures: 6% of EHCPs met the 20-week target in 2025/26; approximately 1,600 overdue EHCPs falling to 740; around 150-300 plans a month processed
findings.quote: the number of EHCPs over 20 weeks old falling from approximately 1,600 to 740 by late Summer 2026

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for External Auditor's Annual Report 2025/26
findings.headline: Funding reform reduces Council income by £44m (31%) in the 2026/27 to 2028/29 MTFP
findings.detail: The paper says the Council intends to offset the reduction through council tax increases at the level expected by government, which it puts at 5%, and through savings plans. The MTFP was approved by Cabinet in February 2026.
findings.matters: A finance director facing the same grant redistribution can compare the size of the reduction against its own exposure, and a lender sees the scale of the income loss the Council is planning around.
findings.figures: £44m reduction in income; 31%; council tax assumed at 5%
findings.quote: it has quantified the financial impact of funding reform to be a reduction in income of £44m, or 31%.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for External Auditor's Annual Report 2025/26
findings.headline: SEND deficit risk estimated at £212m by 31 March 2029 if no grant were received
findings.detail: The paper says the estimate assumed non-receipt of grant for deficits up to 2026. In the MTFP worst case, the Council would hold £12m of reserves, which the paper says indicates a possible risk of financial failure, though it also says government deficit funding has reduced the exposure.
findings.matters: A lender sees the scale of the unfunded SEND exposure against the reserves base, and a finance director can compare its own worst-case reserves projection.
findings.figures: £212m SEND deficit risk by 31 March 2029; £12m reserves in worst case
findings.quote: The Council has estimated the financial risk linked to SEND deficits to be £212m by 31 March 2029

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for External Auditor's Annual Report 2025/26
findings.headline: Government grant will cover 90% of the high-needs DSG accumulated deficit up to 31 March 2026, leaving the Council 10%
findings.detail: The paper says confirmation of the grant was received in early October 2026, and the Council has set aside monies from the 2025/26 treasury outturn to cover the residual 10%. The grant is expected to continue on a multi-year basis until high-needs costs transfer to the Department for Education.
findings.matters: A finance director with a DSG deficit can compare the 90% grant rate and the set-aside approach, and a lender sees the Council's residual liability on the accumulated deficit as 10%.
findings.figures: 90% of accumulated high-needs deficit funded; 10% residual Council liability
findings.quote: a grant where 90% of the accumulated deficit linked to eligible high-needs block costs will be paid off

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for External Auditor's Annual Report 2025/26
findings.headline: In-house children's homes: full savings expected in a future year, after Ofsted registration delays and recruitment
findings.detail: The paper says the Council plans to open ten in-house children's homes, which drive a saving in the 2025/26 budget. It also says delays in Ofsted registration and recruiting experienced staff mean the full savings are expected in a later year.
findings.matters: A finance director planning a similar in-house placement programme can see the lag between opening homes and realising the saving, which the paper ties to registration and staffing.
findings.figures: ten children's homes planned
findings.quote: Consequently, the full savings and benefits from these homes are likely to be realised in a future year.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for External Auditor's Annual Report 2025/26
findings.headline: Council reports no significant cost pressure in Adult Social Care or Home to School Transport in 2025/26, an improvement on 2024/25
findings.detail: The paper says Temporary Accommodation remains a pressure, and that Looked After Children is now the most significant cost pressure among the Critical 5 demand-led areas. DSG is discussed separately in the paper.
findings.matters: Two of the five demand-led areas that account for c. 70% of the budget easing is a shift a peer can track against its own Critical 5 list.
findings.figures: Critical 5 areas make up c. 70% of the budget
findings.quote: the Council has not experienced significant cost pressures this year in respect of Adult Social Care or Home to School Transport, an improvement compared to 2024/25.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for External Auditor's Annual Report 2025/26
findings.headline: Highways upgrades capital spend of £35m overspent, within a four-year £120m roads programme
findings.detail: The paper says the Council noted it had over-spent on the highways project this year, and that the project is part of a four-year £120m roads investment programme. The paper does not give the size of the overspend.
findings.matters: A finance director managing a multi-year roads programme can compare the overspend profile against its own, and a lender sees a capital overspend that the paper does not quantify.
findings.figures: £35m highways spend in 2025/26; four-year £120m roads investment programme
findings.quote: The Council noted it had over-spent on this project this year

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for External Auditor's Annual Report 2025/26
findings.headline: £156m of a £174m capital programme spent in 2025/26, or 90%, up from 80% the year before
findings.detail: The paper says that delivery was limited mainly by contractor availability rather than funding. The largest components were £35m on highways and £42m on infrastructure to unlock housing development.
findings.matters: A peer comparing capital delivery rates can see a sector-typical constraint, contractor capacity, and a year-on-year improvement in the spend ratio.
findings.figures: £174m capital programme; £156m spent; 90% spent (PY: 80%); £35m highways; £42m housing infrastructure
findings.quote: of which £156m or 90% was spent (PY: 80%).

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for External Auditor's Annual Report 2025/26
findings.headline: Year-end cash and short-term investments of £271m, up from £150m, while borrowings fell to £273m from £281m
findings.detail: The paper attributes the rise in cash mainly to litigation receipts and to early grant receipts of £56m from the Department for Education and HS2 for capital projects. Gross debt against the capital financing requirement was 0.4 : 1 in both years.
findings.matters: A lender can see the Council holding more liquidity and slightly less debt, and a finance director can compare cash held for capital timing against its own position.
findings.figures: £271m cash and short-term investments (£150m prior year); £273m year-end borrowings (£281m prior year); £56m early grant receipts; gross debt to CFR 0.4 : 1
findings.quote: The Council has attributed the substantial increase in cash and short-term investments, in part, due to the funds received as a result of a litigation case and early receipt of grants to the tune of £56m from the Department for Education and HS2

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for External Auditor's Annual Report 2025/26
findings.headline: General fund balance of £335m at 31 March 2026, up £65m year-on-year
findings.detail: The paper says the increase offsets reserves drawn from 2022/23 to 2024/25. The Council has also topped up earmarked reserves to protect against future risks linked to high inflation from conflict in the Middle East.
findings.matters: A finance director compares general fund movement against its own position, and a lender reads it as a measure of the Council's buffer against financial shocks.
findings.figures: £335m general fund balance at 31 March 2026; £65m increase year-on-year; usable reserves £471m (2025-26) against £331m (2024-25)
findings.quote: The Council has a general fund balance of £335m as of 31 March 2026, a £65m increase year-on-year.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for External Auditor's Annual Report 2025/26
findings.headline: A c. £9m favourable treasury management variance followed the investment of a one-off legal case receipt
findings.detail: The paper says a legal outcome with a waste disposal services provider over an energy from waste plant produced a large one-off payment, which was invested and produced un-budgeted treasury returns. The Council intends to spend the one-off funds on leisure capital programmes, subject to Cabinet approval, rather than adding recurrent cost.
findings.matters: A one-off receipt that funded an in-year treasury gain, and is then committed to capital rather than revenue, is a funding approach other councils facing windfalls may compare against.
findings.figures: c. £9m favourable variance in treasury management
findings.quote: resulted in a large one-off monetary benefit to the Council which was invested and then yielded un-budgeted treasury management returns.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for External Auditor's Annual Report 2025/26
findings.headline: 2025/26 outturn shows a surplus of c. £4m against a balanced £535m budget
findings.detail: The paper reports corporate costs and funding of £526m against a £535m budget, giving a surplus for the year of c. £4m. The Council attributes this to savings delivery, demand-led budget management and a c. £9m favourable treasury management variance, offset by children's social care cost pressures.
findings.matters: A year that closes in surplus after a balanced budget, with the drivers split out, gives a benchmark for how a peer's outturn can be explained.
findings.figures: surplus c. £4m; £4.4m actual surplus/(deficit) in key metrics; £526m corporate costs and funding; £535m budget; £521m actual net expenditure
findings.quote: leading to a surplus for the year of c. £4m.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for External Auditor's Annual Report 2025/26
findings.headline: Council delivered £78m of savings in 2025/26 against a required c. £77m
findings.detail: The paper says the savings target was c. £77m, or £71m excluding DSG-related savings, and that the Council achieved £78m, an overachievement of c. 1%. The paper links this delivery to the year's surplus and to the Council's readiness for funding reform.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council can compare a 1% overachievement against its own savings delivery, and a lender can see that the year's surplus rested partly on savings delivery rather than on one-off items.
findings.figures: £78m achieved; c. £77m required; £71m required excluding DSG-related savings; overachievement of c. 1%
findings.quote: In practice the Council achieved £78m of savings, or overachievement of c. 1%.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 External Audit Draft Progress Report 2025/26
findings.headline: Two exit package disclosures corrected in the draft financial statements
findings.detail: The auditor records that one exit package was placed in the 0-19,999 band instead of the 20,000-39,999 band, and that an exit package was omitted from the exit packages table although it appeared in the officers' remuneration table. Both have been updated.
findings.matters: Exit package disclosures are reviewed closely by councils and their auditors, and errors in banding are a common point of correction.
findings.figures: Exit package bands: 0-19,999 and 20,000-39,999
findings.quote: One exit package was presented in the 0-19,999 band instead of the 20,000-39,999 band.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 External Audit Draft Progress Report 2025/26
findings.headline: Scale fee for 2025/26 is £690,616, compared with total audit fees of £802,354 for 2024/25
findings.detail: The 2024/25 total included £130,548 of agreed fee variations, while variations for 2025/26 are shown as to be confirmed. The auditor lists anticipated variations for the triennial pension valuation, new auditing standards, prior period adjustments and rebuilding assurance, all subject to PSAA approval.
findings.matters: Fee variations driven by rebuilding assurance and prior period adjustments are costs that councils with disclaimed or restated accounts will also see.
findings.figures: 2025/26 scale fee: £690,616; 2024/25 scale fee: £671,806; 2024/25 fee variations agreed: £130,548; 2024/25 total audit fees: £802,354; anticipated variations: triennial valuation c. £7k, new auditing standards c. £2k, prior period adjustments c. £5k, rebuilding assurance c. £35k
findings.quote: Our fees for the year ending 31 March 2026 are set out in the PSAA Scale Fees communication and are shown below.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 External Audit Draft Progress Report 2025/26
findings.headline: Auditor's prior recommendation on root causes of financial pressures in monitoring reports is marked partially implemented
findings.detail: The auditor says the Council has set out analysis to its corporate management team, particularly on the Critical 5, but would benefit from establishing the root cause of financial pressures in Cabinet reports. Of the 2024-25 recommendations, both procurement and risk management are marked implemented.
findings.matters: Root-cause reporting to members is an early warning control that finance directors elsewhere are also working to strengthen.
findings.figures: 2024-25 observations: 2 implemented (procurement, risk management); 2023-24 observation: partially implemented
findings.quote: However, we believe the Council would benefit from better establishing the root cause of financial pressures and presenting this within Cabinet reports.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 External Audit Draft Progress Report 2025/26
findings.headline: Corporate plan ended in March 2026 and the new plan took effect in April 2026, with the MTFP not yet showing how it aligns to the new plan
findings.detail: The auditor says the MTFP acknowledges the change of corporate plan but does not set out how it will ensure the new plan can be achieved. Management response says the MTFP 2027/28+ will carry additional narrative linking it to corporate plan objectives, and the MTFP 2028/29+ will embed that principle.
findings.matters: A budget that does not yet link to a new corporate plan is a governance point that other councils replacing their plans may face.
findings.quote: The Council's corporate plan ended in March 2026, with a new plan coming into effect from April 2026.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 External Audit Draft Progress Report 2025/26
findings.headline: Auditor identifies no significant weaknesses in financial sustainability or governance arrangements
findings.detail: The value for money summary shows no significant risks and no significant weaknesses for financial sustainability or governance. The one significant risk identified is in the improving economy, efficiency and effectiveness domain, covering the EHCP service.
findings.matters: Auditor conclusions on financial sustainability are a standard reference point for lenders assessing a council's medium-term position.
findings.figures: Significant value for money risks: 1 (improving economy, efficiency and effectiveness)
findings.quote: Financial sustainability No significant risks identified No significant weaknesses identified

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 External Audit Draft Progress Report 2025/26
findings.headline: Auditor finds no significant weakness in EHCP arrangements, noting new resource and backlog progress after the year end
findings.detail: The auditor says timeliness remains below target but has stabilised, that new resource has produced significant progress in clearing the backlog during 2026/27, and that the Council has begun an action plan for future failures. The bulk of the improvement is evidenced after the year end.
findings.matters: The auditor's reasoning shows what evidence it accepted for recovering a statutory service, which other councils with EHCP backlogs can compare against their own position.
findings.quote: Consequently, we have not identified a significant weakness in arrangements to secure economy, efficiency and effectiveness in the use of resources.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 External Audit Draft Progress Report 2025/26
findings.headline: Auditor identifies a significant value for money risk over Education, Health and Care Plans completed within the statutory 20 week deadline
findings.detail: The paper says performance has been falling for some time and has fallen further through 2024-25 and 2025-26, which has in part led to the Council losing tribunal claims. The Council attributes the decline to a significant increase in demand and shortages of qualified assessors.
findings.matters: EHCP timeliness is a statutory service pressure that many councils with high-needs demand are facing, and the auditor's treatment of it sets a reference for the value for money assessment.
findings.figures: Statutory deadline: 20 weeks
findings.quote: The Council has experienced challenges in completing Education, Health and Care Plans (EHCPs) within the statutory 20 week deadline.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 External Audit Draft Progress Report 2025/26
findings.headline: Pension obligation at 31 March 2026 will reflect the triennial valuation as at 31 March 2025, which the auditor rates as a significant risk
findings.detail: The auditor says the triennial valuation may require the actuary to re-base its estimates, which could correct the defined benefit obligation and affect the asset ceiling. The auditor's draft conclusion is that the actuarial assumptions are balanced overall and within a reasonable range, and the variance on benefits paid is being investigated but is not material.
findings.matters: Pension liabilities can move materially with a triennial revaluation, so other councils with similar fund positions can compare the auditor's view of the assumptions.
findings.quote: The actuary will take account of the results of the new Triennial Valuation as at 31 March 2025 for accounting at 31 March 2026.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 External Audit Draft Progress Report 2025/26
findings.headline: Council revalues land and buildings on a rolling five-year cycle, with indexation applied in intervening years
findings.detail: The auditor rates the valuation of land and buildings as a higher assessed risk because assets not revalued in the year may differ from year-end current value if the indexation is not appropriate. The auditor says it was content with the indexation policy and is confirming that the adjustments were applied correctly, with final queries outstanding.
findings.matters: The rolling model under the 2025/26 CIPFA Code changes is one approach among those councils are choosing, and the auditor's reaction to the indexation policy is useful for others considering the same model.
findings.figures: Revaluation cycle: five years, with annual indexation in the four intervening years
findings.quote: The Authority has adopted a rolling revaluation model which sees all land and buildings revalued over a five year cycle and indexation in the intervening years.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 External Audit Draft Progress Report 2025/26
findings.headline: Investment property portfolio valued at £353m at 31 March 2025, of which £292m is commercial premises
findings.detail: The auditor treats the valuation of investment properties as a significant audit risk, focused on the yield used to convert rental income into value. The auditor used its own valuation specialists to review the valuer's report and says that its review of sample evidence has not highlighted any issues to date.
findings.matters: Commercial property yields drive the asset values on the balance sheet of any council holding an income-generating property portfolio, so the valuation basis is a point of comparison for peers.
findings.figures: Investment property portfolio: £353m at 31 March 2025; commercial premises: £292m; agricultural land: £61m
findings.quote: The Council’s investment property portfolio was valued at £353m at 31 March 2025 and was made up primarily of commercial premises (£292m)

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 External Audit Draft Progress Report 2025/26
findings.headline: Auditor identifies a one-off receipt of compensation from a waste disposal services provider after successful litigation as a significant unusual transaction
findings.detail: The auditor identified the receipt as significant and unusual because of its large and one-off nature. It says it was content with the nature and accounting of the transaction.
findings.matters: A large one-off litigation receipt affects a council's reported income and surplus in a single year, and other councils with similar contract disputes can see how the auditor treated it.
findings.quote: We have identified a significant unusual transaction relating to the receipt of compensation monies from a waste disposal services provider following a successful litigation

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 External Audit Draft Progress Report 2025/26
findings.headline: Council's SAP ledger does not mandate journal authorisation, with an off-system approval process in place instead
findings.detail: The auditor says the SAP configuration does not enforce journal authorisation because of a system limitation, and that the lack of enforced authorisation means the manual approval process could be bypassed. The Council has an off-system authorisation process in place and says its design is sufficient for its own purposes. The auditor has identified 24 higher-risk journal entries for detailed testing and has not identified any matters of concern so far.
findings.matters: Any council running SAP without enforced journal approval faces the same control gap, and the auditor's assessment of the workaround is a reference point for peers.
findings.figures: 24 higher-risk journal entries requiring detailed testing
findings.quote: However, the lack of system enforced authorisation means a malicious user could bypass the manual approval process.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 External Audit Draft Progress Report 2025/26
findings.headline: Auditor reports nil uncorrected misstatements and zero control deficiencies to date
findings.detail: The progress report records no uncorrected misstatements in revenues, surplus, total assets or total reserves, and no uncorrected disclosure misstatements. It also records zero significant and zero other control deficiencies. The paper notes that findings remain subject to revision as the work continues.
findings.matters: A clean interim position on misstatements and control deficiencies is a benchmark other councils can compare against their own audit outcomes.
findings.figures: Revenues, surplus for the year, total assets and total reserves: nil (shown as -); significant control deficiencies: 0; other control deficiencies: 0
findings.quote: Our findings are subject to revision as we complete our work

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 External Audit Draft Progress Report 2025/26
findings.headline: Auditor cannot yet confirm the form of audit report, pending work to rebuild assurance over disclaimed periods
findings.detail: The auditor says it will not confirm the form of audit report until all audit work is complete, including the work to rebuild assurance over the disclaimed periods. The paper also lists a fee variation for work to issue a non-standard opinion.
findings.matters: A non-standard opinion would be a visible audit outcome for lenders and for other councils working through disclaimed accounts.

findings.quote: We are on track to sign our audit report before the backstop date.

findings.paper_title: Report for Treasury Management Mid- Year Report 2026/27
findings.headline: Council flags that about 23% of its borrowing matures in the 2-to-5-year period, with new external borrowing needed there as internal borrowing may run out.
findings.detail: The paper says the liability benchmark is not projected to exceed outstanding loans until after the current MTFP period. It identifies the 2-to-5-year window as the point where careful consideration of new external borrowing will be needed.
findings.matters: A large maturity bulge in a short window signals refinancing demand that lenders and other councils will want to track against PWLB and market pricing.

findings.paper_title: Report for Treasury Management Mid- Year Report 2026/27
findings.headline: Council expects no new external borrowing in 2026/27 because its positive cash position covers the capital programme.
findings.detail: The council is under-borrowed against its capital financing requirement by £384.46m, and the paper says internal borrowing has limited reliance on external debt. At 30 September 2026 the council held £293.67m of cash against £252.81m of loans, a net investment position of £40.86m.
findings.matters: A council holding a net investment position while under-borrowed shows how far internal borrowing has been used to avoid external debt, a choice peers with similar capital programmes may be weighing.
findings.figures: Cash £293.67m; loans £252.81m; net investment £40.86m; under-borrowed by £384.46m; forecast new borrowing £0.00m
findings.quote: The positive cash position means that no new borrowing is expected to be undertaken in 2026/27, which would otherwise utilise the budgeted prudential headroom.

findings.paper_title: Report for Treasury Management Mid- Year Report 2026/27
findings.headline: Net financing need for 2026/27 revised to £4.04m from £7.14m, with total capital expenditure forecast at £195.69m against £204.09m.
findings.detail: Capital receipts forecast is £17.68m against £23.77m, and capital grants £135.58m against £149.75m. Capital reserves funding rises to £38.39m from £23.43m. The paper says capital forecasts have been updated for amendments to the programme and in-year operational activity.
findings.matters: A fall in the net borrowing requirement with a rise in reserves funding shows how the funding mix for the capital programme moved, which bears on the council's borrowing need.
findings.figures: Total capital expenditure £195.69m revised (£204.09m original); net financing need £4.04m (£7.14m original); capital receipts £17.68m (£23.77m); capital grants £135.58m (£149.75m); capital reserves £38.39m (£23.43m)
findings.quote: Forecasts for 2026/27 have been updated in line with amendments made to date on the Capital Programme and in-year operational activity.

findings.paper_title: Report for Treasury Management Mid- Year Report 2026/27
findings.headline: Year-end cash forecast revised to £232.32m from £179.30m, £53.02m higher, citing capital programme revisions and slippage in expenditure.
findings.detail: The paper also says the government has confirmed £38.52m of DSG deficit grant funding, which the council expects to receive at the end of November. The DSG grant was not in the original forecast.
findings.matters: A DSG deficit grant of this size, confirmed late in the year, affects how a council funds its high-needs deficit, which finance directors elsewhere are working through.
findings.figures: Revised year-end cash £232.32m; original £179.30m; difference £53.02m; DSG deficit grant £38.52m
findings.quote: The revised forecast for the end of year position is £53.02m higher than originally estimated due to revisions in the Capital Programme and anticipated slippage in expenditure.

findings.paper_title: Report for Treasury Management Mid- Year Report 2026/27
findings.headline: Council's £20m CCLA property fund investment was valued at £18.44m at 30 September 2026, a reduction of £0.35m on the same point last year.
findings.detail: The paper attributes the decline to the Bank of England holding its base rate at 3.75% and signalling a possible rise, which has led institutions to move away from commercial property. The dividend yield on net asset value is 4.74%. The council holds a £1m investment risk reserve against valuation movements, and the IFRS 9 statutory override now runs to 31 March 2029.
findings.matters: Valuation falls on pooled property funds that are subject to the IFRS 9 override affect the General Fund, and other councils holding similar funds will face the same exposure when the override ends.
findings.figures: Investment £20m; valuation at 30 September 2026 £18.44m; reduction £0.35m; dividend yield 4.74%; risk reserve £1m; override extended to 31 March 2029
findings.quote: The value of the Council’s investment as of 30th September 2026 was £18.44m, a reduction of £0.35m from the same period last year.

findings.paper_title: Report for Treasury Management Mid- Year Report 2026/27
findings.headline: Local authority deposits placed in 2026/27 average a 4.73% return against a 4.12% average offered by banks and building societies at placement.
findings.detail: Total deposits placed to date will yield £4.09m, which the paper says is an additional £0.52m over the full term, of which £0.42m falls in 2026/27. The council has reached its £100m limit for deposits with other local authorities, and the first maturities fall in November 2026.
findings.matters: A council that has reached its own cap on lending to peers, and has reopened that market, shows how a new governance route changed short-term returns.
findings.figures: Average local authority return 4.73%; bank and building society average 4.12%; additional yield £0.52m (of which £0.42m in 2026/27); total deposits yield £4.09m; limit £100m
findings.quote: The average return on local authority investments was 4.73% compared to an average of 4.12% offered by banks/ building societies at the time the deposit was placed.

findings.paper_title: Report for Treasury Management Mid- Year Report 2026/27
findings.headline: Treasury budget lines forecast a £17.09m favourable variance for 2026/27 against a £7.70m net budget.
findings.detail: The forecast is driven by higher treasury investment income, with the paper citing elevated returns on term deposits and money market funds. External interest cost is also forecast to be underspent as the council continues internal borrowing.
findings.matters: Investment income and interest cost moving this far from budget shows how a council's treasury position can offset service pressure, which a finance director elsewhere would want to compare.
findings.figures: Net budget £7.70m; forecast net position -£9.39m; favourable variance £17.09m; treasury investment income forecast £13.47m against £1.15m budget; external interest cost forecast £7.27m against £12.24m budget
findings.quote: A favourable variance of £17.09m against these specific budget lines is forecast for the year.

findings.paper_title: Report for Treasury Management Mid- Year Report 2026/27
findings.headline: Council repaid a £15.00m LOBO loan to Dexia Credit Local in July 2026 after the lender exercised its option to increase the rate.
findings.detail: The paper says the council also repaid £3.63m of PWLB borrowing in the first six months. It does not give the original coupon, the proposed rate, the cost of replacement funding or the original maturity of the LOBO. The remaining LOBO of £15.00m has its next call date in July 2029.
findings.matters: A LOBO repayment is a cash and refinancing event, and a finance director at another council will want to know how much replacement funding it required.
findings.figures: £15.00m LOBO repaid; £3.63m PWLB repaid; remaining LOBO £15.00m; next LOBO call July 2029
findings.quote: The Council repaid £3.63m of borrowing to the PWLB in the first six months of 2026/27 and a £15.00m LOBO loan in July to Dexia Credit Local when the lender exercised its option to increase the rate due to be paid.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 Buckinghamshire Pension Fund Statement of Accounts 2025/26
findings.headline: The actuary's sensitivity figures put a one-year rise in assumed life expectancy at £132m on the liability, and a 0.1% increase in the discount rate at a £59m fall.
findings.detail: The paper sets out sensitivities for the actuarial present value of promised retirement benefits. It also gives smaller sensitivities for earnings inflation and for pension increases and deferred revaluation.
findings.matters: These figures show how much the reported liability moves with each assumption, which is the basis for the funding discussions finance directors have with actuaries.

findings.quote: A one-year increase in assumed life expectancy would increase the liability by approximately £132m.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 Buckinghamshire Pension Fund Statement of Accounts 2025/26
findings.headline: Contributors fell to 25,880 at 31 March 2026 from 26,503, while pensioners and dependents rose to 25,973 from 24,773.
findings.detail: Total membership rose to 91,224 from 90,694, with the rise coming from pensioners and dependents. Deferred pensioners fell slightly to 33,012.
findings.matters: A shift from contributors to pensioners changes the fund's cash flow profile and maturity, which affects contribution and funding strategy at employers.

findings.matters: Rising outflows of transfer values reduce the assets the fund holds, and a backlog of unpaid transfers is a timing and liquidity item for the administering authority.

findings.matters: The move of a fund of about £4.7bn from one pool to another is a live change in investment governance that peer funds and employers will be watching.

findings.headline: The Fund wrote its Brunel Pension Partnership share capital down to nil, from £0.84m.
findings.detail: The paper says the write-down follows a government decision that Brunel's response to the Fit for the Future LGPS consultation was unsatisfactory, and that Buckinghamshire was invited to identify another pool. It says several other formerly Brunel funds took the same step.
findings.matters: Councils leaving a pool face a write-off of their share capital and a transition of assets, so other finance officers in pooling arrangements will watch the cost and timing.
findings.figures: £0.84m (share capital written down to nil)

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 Buckinghamshire Pension Fund Statement of Accounts 2025/26
findings.headline: Net returns on investments were £438,745k in 2025/26, against £149,350k in 2024/25, with profits and changes in market value of £406,043k.
findings.detail: The paper attributes the swing to more varied market conditions in 2025/26 than in 2024/25. It says the net positive return helps the Fund continue to meet its future liabilities.
findings.matters: Investment returns drive how far employers' contributions need to fund the gap to liabilities, which is a central concern for any council carrying an LGPS deficit or surplus.
findings.quote: The profit or loss on disposal of investments and changes in the market value of investments reflects the more varied market conditions for the 2025/26 year compared to 2024/25

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 Buckinghamshire Pension Fund Statement of Accounts 2025/26
findings.headline: Fund value at 31 March 2026 stood at £4.711 billion, a 9.9% increase from the balance at 31 March 2025.
findings.detail: The net assets statement gives net assets available to fund benefits of £4,739,106k at 31 March 2026, against £4,310,922k a year earlier. Note 1 quotes the £4.711 billion figure, which differs from the statement total.
findings.matters: A finance director at an LGPS administering authority, or a peer council, would track the growth of the fund's asset base against its employer contribution and funding position.
findings.quote: The Fund value at 31 March 2026 stood at £4.711 billion, a 9.9% increase from the balance at 31 March 2025.

findings.detail: KPMG tested the data given to the actuary and, with its own actuarial specialists, assessed the discount rate, inflation and mortality assumptions. It concluded that the actuarial assumptions are considered reasonable.
findings.matters: A finance director compares triennial valuation outcomes and their assumptions across funds, and KPMG's review of the assumptions is what they would ask for.

findings.detail: The paper lists nil adjusted audit differences. It states that there are no uncorrected misstatements above £2.3 million, and that any uncorrected items would not affect the opinion individually or in aggregate.
findings.matters: Clean misstatement figures are the core of the auditor's assurance, and a peer finance officer can compare them with their own fund's year end.
findings.figures: £2.3m reporting threshold for uncorrected misstatements; nil adjusted audit differences
findings.quote: There are no uncorrected misstatements greater than £2.3 million to report.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 2025-26 Buckinghamshire Pension Fund AFR- DRAFT
findings.headline: Level 3 pooled investment vehicles were valued at £1,138,808k at 31 March 2026, 24.2% of the portfolio, up from £1,042,578k at 31 March 2025 (24.3%).
findings.detail: KPMG tested Level 3 valuations against unaudited NAV statements and the audited accounts of the underlying funds. It reports no audit adjustments for Level 3 assets and no significant variances.
findings.matters: Level 3 holdings rely on unobservable inputs, so a finance director at a peer fund would want to see how large they are and that the auditor found them supportable.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 2025-26 Buckinghamshire Pension Fund AFR- DRAFT
findings.headline: The Fund's asset pooling arrangement moved from Brunel Pension Partnership to London CIV with effect from 1 April 2026, after the year end.
findings.detail: KPMG obtained confirmations from Brunel for the investments held during 2025/26. The paper also refers to a number of investment transitions between managers during the year, which KPMG treated as an audit risk to completeness, existence and accuracy.
findings.matters: A change of pool operator with a live transition is a structural change other administering authorities in pools are also managing.
findings.quote: asset pooling arrangement transitioned from Brunel Pension Partnership to London CIV.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 2025-26 Buckinghamshire Pension Fund AFR- DRAFT
findings.headline: One of two prior-year control recommendations has been implemented, with the declarations of interest for former Audit and Governance Committee members now retained.

Declarations for committee members as of 31 March 2026 have been sent to KPMG and will be kept with the year-end working papers. KPMG inspected them and removed the deficiency.
findings.matters: Retaining declarations of interest after members leave office is a control a finance director can check directly, and this paper shows it being closed out.

findings.detail: KPMG reports journals are approved by email, with no system-based workflow and no formal policy setting roles or thresholds. Management said SAP cannot support system-based approvals, and proposed setting roles and thresholds in the scheme of delegation and including workflow in any new ERP system.
findings.matters: Email-based journal approval without thresholds is a control gap that other councils running SAP may also face, and it shows how an ERP limitation affects a pension fund's control environment.

findings.quote: journals are prepared and approved via email

findings.matters: Management override of controls is a default significant risk in every audit, so an open journal testing item is one a finance director would expect to see closed before sign-off.

findings.paper_title: Report for Treasury Management Annual Report 2025/26
findings.headline: £43m one-off HS2 funding inflates cash position; underlying operational cash generation weaker
findings.detail: Council's cash improved £118.85m during year, but material portion came from one-off receipts: £43m HS2 funding for South East Aylesbury Link Road, £13.38m advance grant receipt, and favourable litigation settlement. Without these one-off items, underlying operational cash generation is substantially lower.
findings.matters: One-off receipts inflate reported cash position; sustainable cash generation is lower than headline position suggests, affecting reliability of budget plans.
findings.figures: £43m HS2 funding; £118.85m total cash increase
findings.quote: £43m of funding received from HS2 for the South East Aylesbury Link Road (SEALR)

findings.paper_title: Report for Treasury Management Annual Report 2025/26
findings.headline: New lending strategy targets other councils with financial stress indicators as counterparties
findings.detail: For 2026/27, the council approved lending surplus cash to other local authorities. By 31 May 2026, four £10m deposits placed with other councils. Council applies enhanced due diligence checking for Section 114 notices, Best Value notices, and Exceptional Financial Support requests – all indicators of financial distress.
findings.matters: Lending to councils with stress indicators introduces significant counterparty credit risk; council deposits could be at risk if any recipient authority faces severe financial difficulty.

Additional due diligence will be undertaken for each local authority with special consideration given to factors including but not limited to the issuance of Section 114 and Best Value notices, requests for Exceptional Financial Support

findings.paper_title: Report for Treasury Management Annual Report 2025/26
findings.headline: Investment income outperformed budget by £9.19m due to temporary interest rate factors; reversal risk ahead
findings.detail: Council earned £11.15m in treasury investment income against budget of £1.96m. Outperformance attributed to higher-than-expected cash balances and interest rates falling more slowly than forecast. As cash normalizes and interest rates potentially fall further, this outperformance will reverse.
findings.matters: The massive swing (£9.19m) indicates the council's investment income forecast is unreliable and dependent on interest rate assumptions, creating risk to next year's funding plan.
findings.figures: £11.15m actual vs £1.96m budget; £9.19m outperformance
findings.quote: Investment returns have exceeded forecasts as a result of additional cash receipts received in year and slower than expected reductions in interest rates

findings.detail: The council invested £20m in the CCLA Local Authority Property Fund; by 31 March 2026 it was valued at £18.75m. The £1.25m loss is mitigated by a £1m reserve approved June 2024. IFRS 9 accounting changes (override expires 31 March 2029) could force additional adverse valuation movements against reserves.
findings.matters: Investment losses erode financial reserves; future accounting changes could force additional charges and reduce the council's financial resilience.

findings.detail: The council forecast it would need to borrow £27.32m in 2025/26 to finance capital spending. Actual result: −£2.98m, meaning no borrowing was needed. This £30m variance suggests either significant capital programme deferral, planning inaccuracy, or changed circumstances. Total capital spend was £155.82m vs £173.82m forecast.
findings.matters: A £30m variance in financing need indicates either capital delivery problems (deferral) or unreliable financial forecasting, both affecting confidence in the council's planning.

findings.paper_title: Report for Treasury Management Annual Report 2025/26
findings.headline: LOBO refinancing decision imminent: £30m borrowing has call date on 28 July 2026
findings.detail: The council holds £30m in LOBO (Lender Option Borrower Option) borrowing with a call date on 28 July 2026. If the lender exercises the option, the council must decide whether to accept a revised interest rate or repay the loan. Financial projections assume the option will be called.
findings.matters: This refinancing decision, happening in days, determines the council's borrowing costs going forward and presents immediate interest rate risk if rates have risen.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2: Year End Report for Audit and Governance Commiittee 2024-25
findings.headline: Investment property portfolio of £347m carries significant valuation uncertainty in retail sector
findings.detail: The Council's investment property portfolio includes commercial units (offices and retail) valued at £347m. Current market conditions carry heightened uncertainty, particularly for retail due to inflation, business rates, and national insurance increases. Auditor's valuation specialists found current judgements balanced, but annual revaluation requirement means continued exposure.
findings.matters: Large asset base vulnerable to market movements. Retail exposure particularly sensitive to economic headwinds. Material downward movement would affect balance sheet strength and borrowing capacity.
findings.figures: Investment property portfolio: £347m
findings.quote: The Council's investment property portfolio of £347m includes a number of commercial units... The valuation is subject to movements based on current market conditions which contain a heightened degree of uncertainty, in particular for the retail sector.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2: Year End Report for Audit and Governance Commiittee 2024-25
findings.headline: EHCP statutory deadline performance significantly deteriorated; High Needs funding under pressure
findings.detail: The Council has experienced sustained challenges completing Education, Health and Care Plans (EHCPs) within the statutory 20-week deadline, with performance significantly deteriorating over 2024/25, resulting in lost tribunal claims. The deterioration is driven by increased demand and shortages of qualified assessors. The auditor notes risk of material unidentified pressure on the High Needs block of Dedicated Schools Grant, which funds EHCP provisions.
findings.matters: Service failure creates reputational and legal risk. Unquantified High Needs pressure could mask additional deficits not currently visible.
findings.figures: Statutory deadline: 20 weeks
findings.quote: The Council has experienced challenges in completing Education, Health and Care Plans (EHCPs) within the statutory 20 week deadline... performance has significantly deteriorated over the course of 2024-25. This has resulted in the Council losing tribunal claims.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2: Year End Report for Audit and Governance Commiittee 2024-25
findings.headline: Control weaknesses in journal entry processing allowing posts without authorisation
findings.detail: The auditor identified weaknesses in the control environment for journal entries, specifically that there are routes by which journal entries can be posted without authorisation or proper segregation of duties. The auditor analysed 38 high-risk journal entries and found no instances of management override, but notes the control gap remains.
findings.matters: Control environment weakness increases risk of error or misstatement going undetected.
findings.figures: 38 high-risk journal entries tested
findings.quote: We identified a weakness in journal entries because there are routes by which journal entries can be posted without authorisation or segregation of duties.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2: Year End Report for Audit and Governance Commiittee 2024-25
findings.headline: £5.4m expected credit loss on subsidiary loan; Consilio Property Ltd in net liability position
findings.detail: The Council has recorded a £5.404m expected credit loss on a loan made to Consilio Property Ltd, a subsidiary. This loss was required because the company is in a net liability position, indicating increased credit risk and risk that the Council will be unable to recover its investment. The Council's procedures for calculating expected credit losses do not currently identify potential defaults on all counterparties.
findings.matters: The Council has capital at risk in a struggling subsidiary. The inadequacy of credit loss assessment processes creates potential for further unidentified losses.
findings.figures: £5,404k expected credit loss recorded
findings.quote: The Council has recorded an expected credit loss (ECL) in respect of a loan made to Consilio Property Ltd because this company is in a net liability position. This indicates an increase in credit risk and therefore a risk that the Council will be unable to recover its investment.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2: Year End Report for Audit and Governance Commiittee 2024-25
findings.headline: £9.4m uncorrected understatement of revenues recorded
findings.detail: The auditor identified a material uncorrected audit misstatement in the financial statements: revenues are understated by £9.401 million (0.6% of total revenues). This misstatement was not corrected before finalisation of the accounts. The auditor has formally requested the Council correct this error in line with ISA standards.
findings.matters: The reported outturn position is materially misstated. This affects both the perceived financial performance and the integrity of budget monitoring.
findings.figures: £9,401k revenue understatement

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2: Year End Report for Audit and Governance Commiittee 2024-25
findings.headline: Auditor disclaiming opinion on entire financial statements for 2024/25
findings.detail: The external auditor cannot provide assurance that the financial statements are free from material misstatement because there was insufficient time to complete work before the statutory backstop date of 27 February 2026. The auditor specifically cites inability to obtain evidence over the split of useable and unusable reserves, which they view as pervasive to the Council's financial position. This follows disclaimers on the prior two years (2022/23 and 2023/24).
findings.matters: Lenders cannot rely on an independently audited financial position. The lack of assurance over reserves is critical to understanding the Council's true financial flexibility and sustainability.
findings.figures: Statutory backstop date: 27 February 2026
findings.quote: We have determined that there is insufficient time to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence over the split of useable and unusable reserves as at 31 March 2025 or 31 March 2024 ahead of the backstop, and, in our view, this is pervasive to the Council's financial position as at 31 March 2025.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for Annual Governance Statement 2025/26
findings.headline: Chief Executive and Chief Internal Auditor departed mid-year; interim arrangements in place
findings.detail: Chief Executive Rachael Shimmin departed in January 2026 after leading most of 2025/26. Chief Internal Auditor Maggie Gibb departed in September 2025. Both interim replacements were appointed. These departures occurred during a period of substantial financial pressure and governance transition.
findings.matters: Leadership continuity in finance and audit oversight is critical; interim arrangements limit experience and authority in key roles overseeing financial controls during period of major funding pressures
findings.figures: CEO departure January 2026; Chief Internal Auditor departure September 2025
findings.quote: The Chief Executive throughout most of 2025/26 was Rachael Shimmin until her departure from the Council in January 2026. Similarly, in September 2025 the Chief Internal Auditor, Maggie Gibb, left the Council which led to the appointment of the Interim Chief Internal Auditor.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for Annual Governance Statement 2025/26
findings.headline: Council received disclaimed audit opinions in prior years; rebuilding toward unmodified opinion by 2027/28
findings.detail: The Council's accounts in prior years received disclaimed audit opinions, indicating auditors could not form an opinion on the accounts. A pathway to rebuild assurance was presented in November 2025, with goal of achieving unmodified audit opinion on 2027/28 accounts.
findings.matters: Disclaimed audit opinions signal prior audit failures and suggest weaknesses in financial controls or accounting records; rebuilding assurance is essential but until achieved represents unresolved audit risk
findings.figures: Target unmodified opinion by 2027/28 accounts
findings.quote: A pathway to 'building back assurance' on the Council's accounts following prior years' disclaimed audit opinions was presented to Audit and Governance committee in November 2025. The goal of this process is the issue of an unmodified opinion on the Council's published 2027/28 accounts.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for Annual Governance Statement 2025/26
findings.headline: Government's Fair Funding Review will reduce funding by £44.4m by 2028/29
findings.detail: The Government's Fair Funding Review will significantly reduce funding from 2026/27. The Council states its Medium Term Financial Plan balances over the 3-year period, but achieving this with a £44.4m reduction will require difficult decisions and substantial savings.
findings.matters: A £44.4m reduction in government funding is material and will force significant service reductions or additional borrowing; a lender needs assurance the Council can manage this gap without destabilizing finances
findings.figures: £44.4m reduction by 2028/29
findings.quote: The Government's Fair Funding Review will impact the Council's financial position from 2026/27 and will result in a reduction in Government funding received by the Council of £44.4m by 2028/29.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1: Auditor's Annual Report for Buckinghamshire Council 2024-25 (1)
findings.headline: Investment properties valued at £347m carry significant valuation risk due to market uncertainty and sensitivity to accounting assumptions.
findings.detail: The council holds investment properties valued at £347m, required to be revalued annually by external surveyors. The size of the balance combined with market uncertainty and sensitive underlying assumptions creates significant risk of valuation error. The auditor's limited procedures found no material misstatements but the risk remains.
findings.matters: A material revaluation error could significantly impact the council's net asset position; market downturns could force impairments affecting borrowing capacity.
findings.figures: £347m in investment properties held at fair value
findings.quote: Whilst the Council does use an established firm of chartered surveyors to determine fair value, the size of the balance (£347m) combined with uncertainty in market conditions and the impact of sensitive assumptions means the risk of error in the valuation is significant.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1: Auditor's Annual Report for Buckinghamshire Council 2024-25 (1)
findings.headline: Internal audit raised significant concerns about procurement function effectiveness, with critical report in 2023-24, and improvements remain unverified.
findings.detail: Over two years, internal audit raised concerns about procurement effectiveness, culminating in a critical contract management report in Q4 2023-24. The council restructured procurement teams and systems ahead of the Procurement Act coming into force in February 2025, but has not obtained assurance that previous weaknesses have been resolved.
findings.matters: Weak procurement controls increase risk of wasteful spending and poor value for money; unverified improvements mean weaknesses may persist.
findings.figures: Critical internal audit report Q4 2023-24; Procurement Act implementation February 2025
findings.quote: Over the past two years, the Council's internal auditors has raised concerns about the effectiveness of the procurement function, with a particularly critical report in respect of contract management issued in the final quarter of the 2023/24 financial year.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1: Auditor's Annual Report for Buckinghamshire Council 2024-25 (1)
findings.headline: Education, Health and Care Plan assessment service has significantly deteriorated, missing statutory 20-week deadlines and losing tribunal claims.
findings.detail: The auditor identified the EHCP service as carrying a significant value for money risk. Performance deteriorated substantially over 2024-25, driven by demand growth and shortages of qualified assessors. The council has lost tribunal claims and suffered reputational damage. While a SEND recovery board was established by year-end, it is not yet fully embedded.
findings.matters: Service failures indicate weak operational management; the EHCP backlog represents unquantified additional costs that could materially worsen the DSG position beyond the current £25m deficit.
findings.figures: Performance deteriorated significantly over 2024-25; SEND Board established by 31 March 2025
findings.quote: The Council has experienced challenges in completing Education, Health and Care Plans (EHCPs) within the statutory 20 week deadline. The Council's performance has been deteriorating for some time, similar to other authorities, but significantly deteriorated over the course of 2024-25.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1: Auditor's Annual Report for Buckinghamshire Council 2024-25 (1)
findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant high-needs deficit has reached £25m with rapid acceleration, and the statutory override masking it expires in March 2028.
findings.detail: The accumulated DSG deficit stood at £25m as at 31 March 2025, a jump of £18m from the prior year. The council is using a statutory override to avoid recognizing it against usable reserves, but this override expires in March 2028. A backlog in completing Education, Health and Care Plan assessments creates risk of further unquantified cost pressures on this grant.
findings.matters: This represents a real and growing liability that will impact usable reserves once the override expires; the EHCP backlog suggests the full underlying cost has not yet materialized.
findings.figures: £25m accumulated DSG deficit as at 31 March 2025; increase of £18m from prior year; override expires March 2028
findings.quote: The accumulated deficits in DSG as at 31 March 2025 is £25m, an increase of £18m since the prior period and a rapid acceleration since recent years.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1: Auditor's Annual Report for Buckinghamshire Council 2024-25 (1)
findings.headline: Auditor issued a disclaimer of opinion on the council's financial statements due to inability to obtain sufficient audit evidence before the statutory deadline.
findings.detail: The auditor could not obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence across multiple material areas by the statutory backstop date of 27 February 2026, including land and buildings valuations, infrastructure asset categorization, fees and charges income, non-current asset revaluations, and the full position on usable and unusable reserves. As a result, no audit opinion was issued on the 2024-25 financial statements.
findings.matters: A disclaimer of opinion means the auditor cannot verify the financial statements give a true and fair view of the council's financial position, making them unreliable as a basis for lending decisions.
findings.figures: Disclaimer issued 2 February 2026; statutory backstop date 27 February 2026
findings.quote: We issued a disclaimer of opinion on the Council's financial statements on 2 February 2026. This is because we have been unable to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence over the financial statements on account of the statutory backstop date.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Strategy Statement 2026-27 10.02.26
findings.headline: Significant debt maturing from 2028 onwards, requiring new borrowing into uncertain rate environment
findings.detail: From 2028, the council forecasts that both its net loans requirement and liability benchmark will exceed outstanding loans, driven by substantial debt maturing. This means refinancing risk: large sums of fixed-rate PWLB debt coming due when they must be refinanced into whatever interest-rate environment prevails at that time. The Liability Benchmark chart (Graph A and B) illustrates the scale.
findings.matters: Refinancing of maturing debt in an uncertain rate environment creates a material exposure; if rates are higher than today's estimates, the council's financing costs will rise sharply.
findings.figures: PI 5 Borrowing Limits Authorised Limit 2028/29: £384.00m; PI 8 maturity table shows material amounts falling due in each period thereafter
findings.quote: Both the Net Loans Requirement and the Liability Benchmark are projected to exceed the value of outstanding loans from 2028 due to a significant amount of debt maturing as demonstrated in Prudential Indicator 8, paragraph 4.12, and net expenditure exceeding income as demonstrated in Prudential Indicator 6, paragraph 5.3.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Strategy Statement 2026-27 10.02.26
findings.headline: Cumulative Dedicated Schools Grant deficit anticipated to grow significantly across medium-term financial plan
findings.detail: The document identifies the growing DSG deficit as one of two primary drivers of cash depletion (alongside capital programme spend). DSG deficits are statutory—councils cannot discharge them and they accumulate on the balance sheet, creating a structural pressure on finances that grows year on year.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether cash is being consumed by discretionary capital choices or by statutory pressures that cannot be controlled; a growing DSG deficit is the latter and signals tightening headroom.
findings.figures: DSG deficit identified as a 'primary driver' of reducing cash balance but specific figures not quantified in this document
findings.quote: The primary drivers of the reducing cash balance are the forecast net financing requirement of the capital programme (approximately £48 million as per the forecast provided on 9th December 2025) and the impact of the cumulative deficit on the Dedicated Schools Grant, which is anticipated to grow significantly across the MTFP period.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Strategy Statement 2026-27 10.02.26
findings.headline: Capital financing cost jumps to 5.95% of revenue in 2026/27, nearly double the prior year
findings.detail: The affordability indicator—the ratio of capital financing costs (borrowing and long-term obligations) to net revenue—spikes from 3.23% in 2025/26 to 5.95% in 2026/27, then again to 5.03% in 2028/29. This reflects both lower investment returns (as interest rates fall) and increased revenue funding for capital. The spike signals financing costs are consuming growing portions of available revenue.
findings.matters: This ratio drives whether a council can sustain its capital programme within revenue capacity. A spike to 5.95% flags when financing costs become more onerous relative to income.
findings.quote: The primary reasons for the projected increase in the ratio in future years are twofold: a decrease in investment income, which aligns with the forecasted bank base rate, and an increase in revenue funding for capital projects.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Strategy Statement 2026-27 10.02.26
findings.headline: Cash reserves to fall from £193m to £41m by 2028/29, forcing first external borrowing from 2027/28
findings.detail: The council currently finances capital via cash reserves (internal borrowing) rather than external loans, an under-borrowed position of £365m. But cash is declining sharply. The forecast shows closing balances of £193m (2025/26), £114m (2026/27), £64m (2027/28), £41m (2028/29). Once depleted, the council will need to borrow externally for the first time in years.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand when the council shifts from internally funded to externally dependent; this marks that inflection point and signals need to assess new borrowing capacity.
findings.quote: Based on current assumptions, the Council is likely to require external borrowing for the first time in 2027/28. The primary drivers of the reducing cash balance are the forecast net financing requirement of the capital programme (approximately £48 million as per the forecast provided on 9th December 2025) and the impact of the cumulative deficit on the Dedicated Schools Grant, which is anticipated to grow significantly across the MTFP period.

news_drafts.headline: Buckinghamshire repaid a £15.00m LOBO loan in July after lender Dexia raised the rate
news_drafts.lead:
Buckinghamshire Council repaid a £15.00m LOBO loan to Dexia Credit Local in July 2026, after the lender exercised its option to increase the rate. A LOBO is a bank loan where, on set dates, the lender may propose a higher interest rate and the council may then repay the loan in full instead of accepting it. The repayment is reported in the treasury management mid-year report for 2026/27, which goes to the Audit and Governance Committee on 10 November.

The council also repaid £3.63m of borrowing to the Public Works Loan Board, the government's lending arm for councils, in the first six months of 2026/27. The paper does not give the loan's original interest rate, the rate the lender proposed, the cost of replacement funding or the date the LOBO was due to mature.

A further LOBO of £15.00m remains. Its next call date, the next date on which the lender may propose a new rate, is July 2029.
